items.prompt: Two disjoint singly linked lists are sorted in nondecreasing order. Existing nodes must be reused to build one sorted result. Which maintained state directly supports the merge?
constraints: Both inputs are acyclic, sorted, and node-disjoint.
No replacement data nodes may be allocated.

options.text: References to each current unmerged head and to the last node of the merged output.
A fast/slow pointer pair on each input.
A frequency table of values with no node references.
Random-access midpoint indices for both lists.

feedback.reason: Sortedness makes the two current heads the only candidates for the next output node, while tail records where to attach it.

blocks.text: All nodes behind an input head are at least as large as that head, so comparing the two heads is sufficient. Appending the chosen existing node to tail and advancing only its source preserves both sortedness and reachability. Midpoint indices are unavailable, a value table loses node identity, and fast/slow convergence solves a different structural problem.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_midpoints: Singly linked lists do not provide direct midpoint access, and merging needs the smallest remaining front, not a midpoint.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.value_frequency_only: Values alone cannot reuse or preserve the original node objects required by the contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cycle_meeting: Relative-speed traversal does not choose the next sorted candidate or maintain the output tail.

items.prompt: During a node-reusing merge of two sorted lists, select all statements that form the loop invariant immediately before the next comparison.
constraints: Input nodes are reused and each input is individually sorted.
The output is built by next-link attachment at tail.

options.text: tail must always be the node with the larger current payload.
l1 and l2 are null or reference the first not-yet-selected node of each input.
The chain ending at tail contains exactly the already selected nodes in sorted order.
Both l1 and l2 must have advanced on every prior iteration.

feedback.reason: The merge partitions nodes into one sorted output prefix and two intact unconsumed suffixes.

blocks.text: tail marks the last node already committed to the output. l1 and l2 retain the entry references to all remaining nodes, so choosing the smaller head is safe and loses no suffix. Only the source that supplied the chosen node advances. tail's payload need not be the larger current input; it is the largest value already emitted under nondecreasing order.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tail_is_larger_input: tail belongs to the emitted prefix and is not selected as the larger of the two current candidates.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.both_sources_advance: Advancing both would skip the unchosen input node and lose it from the result.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.merged_prefix_sorted: Without sorted-prefix correctness, choosing a head cannot establish the result order.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.sources_at_first_unmerged: Without intact source frontiers, unselected nodes can be skipped or duplicated.

items.prompt: During a sorted merge, l1 becomes null while l2 references X -> Y -> Z, an intact sorted suffix. tail is the last output node. What is the correct completion step?
constraints: l2 is an intact sorted suffix.
The two inputs are disjoint and acyclic.

options.text: Reverse X -> Y -> Z before attachment.
Copy X.value into tail and discard X, Y, and Z.
Set tail.next = l2 and finish.
Advance l1 until it becomes non-null again.

feedback.reason: The remaining l2 suffix is already sorted and all of its nodes are still reachable from l2, so one link preserves the entire remainder.

blocks.text: All values in the emitted prefix are no greater than the current remaining candidates. Once l1 is exhausted, no future comparison is needed; l2's internal order is already valid. Linking tail.next to l2 retains every remaining node. Copying one value loses identities and nodes, null cannot advance, and reversing would violate nondecreasing order.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.copy_first_only: This drops the remaining node chain and violates node reuse and completeness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.advance_null: A null source has no successor and cannot become non-null by traversal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.reverse_remainder: The suffix is already in the required order; reversing it makes the result unsorted.

items.prompt: A merge initializes dummy and tail = dummy, attaches all selected data nodes through tail.next, and completes successfully. Which return value satisfies a contract that excludes implementation sentinels?
constraints: dummy is not part of the logical data model.
The merged result is singly linked from its first data node.

options.text: Return the original first-list head regardless of which input node was selected first.
Return tail, which is the last data node.
Return dummy so its payload becomes the first result value.
Return dummy.next, the first selected data node in the merged result.

feedback.reason: dummy.next is the first selected data node, while dummy itself is only the stable anchor used during construction.

blocks.text: The sentinel removes the first-attachment special case because tail always designates an existing node. It does not change which data node is smallest or become part of the requested result. tail ends at the last node, not the head, and the original l1 head may not be first. Returning dummy.next exposes exactly the constructed logical chain.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dummy_itself: This leaks implementation scaffolding into a result whose contract excludes the sentinel.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tail_only: The tail reference cannot reach earlier nodes in a singly linked result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.original_l1: The first output node is determined by values and emptiness, not by which input was named first.

items.prompt: Two disjoint sorted singly linked lists contain m and n nodes. A merge reuses nodes, compares current heads, and appends the untouched remainder. What are the time and extra-space costs?
constraints: Input nodes are reused rather than copied.
The inputs are already sorted and acyclic.

feedback.reason: Every input node is consumed at most once through sequential links, and only a fixed set of head/tail references is retained.

blocks.text: The loop advances one source pointer per selected node and then attaches one remaining suffix. Across both inputs, at most m+n nodes are processed, yielding O(m+n) time. A dummy, tail, l1, and l2 are constant auxiliary references, so extra space is O(1). No random-access insertion or element shifting is involved.

items.prompt: l1 references X(value=4) and l2 references Y(value=4). X and Y are distinct nodes, and the output must contain every input node. What should the merge do at this tie?
constraints: X and Y are separately allocated and the input lists are disjoint.
The merge is not a deduplication operation.

options.text: Allocate one new node with value 4 and discard X and Y.
Include only one because equal values mean X and Y are the same node.
Attach X and set X.next = X to record both equal occurrences.
Choose one according to the declared tie rule, advance only that source, and later include the other node too.

feedback.reason: Equal payloads create an ordering tie, not an identity equivalence; completeness requires both distinct nodes.

blocks.text: A deterministic tie rule—often choosing from the first list—can preserve stability, but either choice is compatible with sortedness if specified. Only the chosen source advances, leaving the other equal-valued node for a later iteration. Collapsing nodes silently changes a merge into deduplication, a self-link creates a cycle, and a replacement loses both original identities.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.collapse_duplicate: Equal payloads do not make separately allocated nodes identical, and the output contract requires every node.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.link_x_to_x: A self-cycle neither represents Y nor produces a valid sorted linear result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.replace_with_new: This violates node reuse and discards two required identities.

items.prompt: chosen references the smaller current source node, chosenNext stores its original successor, and tail is the last output node. Select all structural dependencies required for one safe merge step.
constraints: chosenNext was captured before any chosen.next overwrite.
tail and chosen are distinct before this step.
The next head comparison begins only after this step is complete.

options.text: The old tail must receive tail.next = chosen before tail is reassigned to chosen.
The chosen source head must become chosenNext before the next head comparison.
The chosen source head must advance before the old tail can link to chosen.
chosen.next must be set to null immediately after attachment, even though chosenNext preserves the source suffix.

feedback.reason: Attachment must use the old tail, and the saved successor must become the source frontier before the next comparison; the two state advances have no required order between them.

items: While tail still references the previous output end, assign `tail.next = chosen`; moving tail first and then assigning that expression would set `chosen.next = chosen` and create a self-cycle.
Set `tail = chosen` so the next attachment uses the new output end.
Set the chosen source head to `chosenNext` before the next comparison so the selected node is not considered again.

blocks.text: Steps 2 and 3 may occur in either order because chosenNext already preserves the original source suffix; only the attachment-before-tail-move dependency is strict. Clearing chosen.next is unnecessary and can temporarily sever the saved suffix from the structure. On the next iteration, chosen.next becomes the next selected output edge, or it is linked to the final untouched remainder.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.source_before_attachment: Because chosen and chosenNext are already saved, advancing the source is independent of assigning oldTail.next = chosen.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.clear_chosen_next: The merge needs no null-termination at each iteration; clearing the link adds work and can disconnect the suffix before reconnection.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.attach_before_tail_move: Using the old tail creates the output edge; moving tail first would make tail.next = chosen a self-link.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.advance_source_before_next_comparison: The source frontier must move to chosenNext so the selected node is consumed exactly once.

items.prompt: Two sorted input heads eventually reach the same node S, so their tails are structurally shared. A standard node-reusing merge assumes disjoint inputs. What is the correct assessment?
constraints: S is the same node object on both input paths.
The algorithm reuses nodes and does not clone the shared suffix.

options.text: Adding a dummy output head automatically removes the shared-tail hazard.
Appending S from each source produces two logical copies without allocation.
The standard loop is safe as long as S.value is ordered correctly.
The precondition is violated; the merge must detect the shared suffix and attach it once or reject the input.

feedback.reason: A shared node is one object reachable from both sources, so consuming it twice is not equivalent to consuming two distinct nodes.

blocks.text: The standard invariant partitions disjoint nodes between two unconsumed suffixes. Structural sharing breaks that partition: once one path attaches S, the other source may later designate the same object. Naive updates can duplicate a reference in the logical plan or create a cycle when the tail already reaches S. An alias-aware implementation can stop when l1 is l2 and attach the common suffix once; otherwise the input should be rejected.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.values_make_safe: Sorted payloads do not eliminate identity aliasing or prevent attaching one object twice.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.append_twice: One node object cannot represent two independent occurrences in a linear chain without copying, and repeated attachment can create a cycle.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dummy_fixes_alias: A sentinel simplifies the first output edge but does not change input sharing.

items.prompt: A node-reusing merge receives one empty sorted list and one nonempty sorted list. What should the result contain?

options.text: The nonempty list's existing head and entire suffix, attached without allocating data nodes.
Null because both inputs are required to contribute at least one node.
A copied list because an empty input prevents pointer reuse.
The sentinel node because no comparison was performed.

feedback.reason: An empty sorted input contributes no nodes; the untouched nonempty suffix is already a valid sorted result.

blocks.text: The merge loop can stop when either pointer is null and append the remaining pointer directly. A dummy is scaffolding, not output, and node reuse means the existing suffix can be linked without copying.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.null: The nonempty input still supplies the complete result.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.copy_other: The contract reuses existing nodes and no copy is needed.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dummy_only: The logical result starts at dummy.next.

items.prompt: Two sorted lists share a tail node, but the merge implementation assumes disjoint inputs and reuses nodes. What must be addressed?

options.text: Define whether shared nodes may appear once or twice and guard against creating a cycle or duplicating identity; the disjoint-input proof no longer applies unchanged.
Run the same merge because sortedness prevents any topology issue.
Always copy values without checking whether identity preservation is part of the contract.
Sort the shared tail to remove the alias.

feedback.reason: Shared input identity changes what “append both lists” means and can make naive link rewiring cyclic.

blocks.text: A standard merge assumes each source node is owned by one input and can be selected once. With a shared suffix, selecting it from both pointers can revisit the same node or set a link back into the output. The contract must choose one occurrence, copy, or a specialized intersection-aware merge.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.ignore_sharing: Sorted values do not prevent pointer aliasing or duplicate traversal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.copy_everything: Copying may violate a node-reuse contract and is not a policy decision by itself.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_tail: Sorting values does not remove shared references or fix links.

items.prompt: After a sorted merge loop stops because one input is empty, what must happen to the nonempty remainder?
constraints: The remaining suffix is already sorted.
Nodes may be reused in place.

options.text: Attach the remaining suffix directly to the output tail; no per-node comparison with an empty input is needed.
options.explanation: The invariant already proves the remainder is the next sorted suffix.

options.text: Discard the remainder because the output is complete when one pointer reaches null.
Sort the remaining suffix again before attaching it.
options.explanation: The suffix was already sorted under the merge invariant.

options.text: Copy only the final remaining value into the output.
options.explanation: Every remaining node belongs in the merged result.

feedback.reason: The merge invariant transfers the entire remaining sorted suffix once the other input is exhausted.

blocks.text: At loop termination, all chosen output nodes precede both remaining pointers, and one pointer is null. The nonempty input is already internally ordered, so one link attachment preserves order and linear work.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.resort_remainder: The suffix was already sorted under the merge invariant.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.copy_last_value: Every remaining node belongs in the merged result.

items.prompt: When merging two sorted lists with equal current values, which tie policy is safe under a node-preserving contract?
constraints: Both equal-valued nodes must appear in the output.
Relative order between source lists is not specified.

options.text: Choose either current node, advance only that source, and preserve the other node for the next comparison.
options.explanation: The important invariants are sortedness and retaining both identities.

options.text: Drop one node because equal values represent the same output element.
options.explanation: Equal payloads do not imply equal node identity.

options.text: Copy the value once into a new node and discard both source nodes.
options.explanation: This violates node reuse and multiplicity.

options.text: Attach one node and advance both sources because their values match.
options.explanation: Advancing both loses one required node.

feedback.reason: A merge tie concerns source order, not whether an equal-valued node may be discarded.

blocks.text: Stable merge may choose a preferred source, but a node-preserving contract requires both nodes to remain reachable exactly once. The unchosen pointer must not advance until its node is attached.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.drop_duplicate: Equal payloads do not imply equal node identity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.copy_value_once: This violates node reuse and multiplicity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.advance_both: Advancing both loses one required node.

items.prompt: Which precondition does the standard two-pointer merge rely on for each input?
constraints: Each input is sorted according to the same ordering.
The merge compares only the current heads.

options.text: After any prefix is consumed, each remaining input suffix is still ordered, so its head is the smallest remaining node from that source.
options.explanation: This makes comparing the two heads sufficient.

options.text: All payloads must be distinct so the smaller head is unambiguous.
options.explanation: Ties are safe when both nodes are preserved.

options.text: The implementation must access arbitrary positions to verify every suffix.
options.explanation: The merge uses sequential next links and the sortedness precondition.

options.text: Inputs must have equal length so pointers advance in lockstep.
options.explanation: Different lengths are handled by attaching the remainder.

feedback.reason: Head comparison is sufficient only because each source head represents the minimum of its remaining ordered suffix.

blocks.text: The merge proof is an invariant about both suffixes. If either input is unsorted, a later node may be smaller than its current head and the two-pointer choice can no longer be locally safe.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.unique_values: Ties are safe when both nodes are preserved.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.random_access: The merge uses sequential next links and the sortedness precondition.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.same_length: Different lengths are handled by attaching the remainder.

items.prompt: What extra policy is required before reusing nodes while merging inputs that share a suffix?
constraints: The same node may be reachable from both heads.
The output must not duplicate identity or create a cycle.

options.text: Detect or explicitly handle the shared suffix so each shared node is attached according to a one-occurrence policy and links remain acyclic.
options.explanation: The ordinary disjoint-input proof does not cover aliases.

options.text: Run the ordinary merge because sortedness guarantees disjoint node identities.
Attach the shared suffix once from each input to preserve both source lists in the output.
options.explanation: One object cannot safely occur twice without an explicit graph-output contract.

options.text: Sort node addresses to make shared identity disappear.
options.explanation: Address order does not remove aliases or define output semantics.

feedback.reason: Shared input topology changes the meaning of node reuse and must be part of the merge contract.

blocks.text: A standard merge assumes disjoint ownership: each source node is selected once. With a shared tail, blindly advancing both pointers can duplicate a node or rewire a cycle. The implementation needs an explicit identity policy before choosing links.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.duplicate_shared_nodes: One object cannot safely occur twice without an explicit graph-output contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.sort_by_address: Address order does not remove aliases or define output semantics.
